lessons.title: Making and indexing lists
lessons.summary: Storing many values under one name.
lessons.notes:
A **list** (OCR calls it an array) stores many values in order.

```python
scores = [10, 20, 30]
print(scores[0])   # 10 - counting starts at 0
scores[1] = 25     # change an item
scores.append(40)  # add to the end
print(len(scores)) # how many items
```

The last item is at index `len(list) - 1`. Going past it gives an *index out of range* error.

Loop over a list either by item or by index:

```python
for score in scores:      # each value
for i in range(len(scores)):  # each position
```
lessons.worked_example:
values = []
for i in range(3):
    values.append(int(input()))
print(values[0])
print(len(values))
lessons.worked_example_note: Start with an empty list and `append()` inside the loop to build it from user input.

lessons.title: Searching, totalling and 2D lists
lessons.summary: Linear search, aggregation and lists of lists.
lessons.notes:
A **linear search** checks each item in turn:

```python
found = False
for item in items:
    if item == target:
        found = True
```

Useful built-ins: `sum(list)`, `max(list)`, `min(list)`, `len(list)`, `sorted(list)`, `list.index(value)`.

A **2D list** is a list of lists — a grid:

```python
grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
print(grid[1][0])  # 3  -> row 1, column 0
```

OCR writes 2D arrays as `array[row][column]`, so read the row first.
lessons.worked_example_note: `in` performs the search for you; `index()` then reports the position. An exam answer may need the loop written out in full.

lessons.title: Exam-style list problems
lessons.summary: Building, filtering and reporting on data sets.
lessons.notes:
Most list questions are a variation of four jobs:

1. **Build** — read values into a list
2. **Search** — find one value or its position
3. **Aggregate** — total, average, biggest, smallest, count how many match
4. **Report** — print the results in a stated format

Decide which jobs the question needs, then write them one after another. Be careful with output order, and whether the question wants the value, the position, or both.
lessons.worked_example_note: Build first, then process. Keeping the two loops separate makes the logic easier to follow and to mark.

tasks.title: First and last
tasks.brief: Input three words, one per line, into a list. Print the first item, then the last item, each on its own line.
hints: Index 0 is the first item. The last item's index is len(items) - 1.
words = [], for i in range(3): words.append(input()), then print(words[0]) and print(words[-1])

tasks.title: List total
tasks.brief: Input four whole numbers, one per line, into a list. Print the total of the list.
hints: Python's built-in sum() adds up every item in a list for you.
numbers = [], for i in range(4): numbers.append(int(input())), then print(sum(numbers))

tasks.title: Print in reverse
tasks.brief: Input four words, one per line, into a list. Print them one per line, in the opposite order to how they were entered.
hints: for item in reversed(words): loops through a list back to front.
words = [], for i in range(4): words.append(input()), then for word in reversed(words): print(word)

tasks.title: Middle word
tasks.brief:
Read a whole number N (this will always be odd). Then read N words, one per line, into a list. Print the middle word — the one exactly in the centre of the list.

For example, if N is 5 and the words are a, b, c, d, e, the middle one is c (there are two words before it and two after).
hints: For a list with an odd number of items, the middle index is len(items) // 2 — integer division rounds down, which lands exactly in the centre for an odd-length list.
n = int(input()), words = [], for i in range(n): words.append(input()), then print(words[n // 2])

tasks.title: Highest and lowest
tasks.brief: A shop records five daily sales figures, entered one per line. Display the highest figure on the first line. Display the lowest figure on the second line.
hints: Python's built-in max() and min() work directly on a list.
sales = [], for i in range(5): sales.append(int(input())), then print(max(sales)) and print(min(sales))

tasks.title: Search a register
tasks.brief:
Five names are entered, one per line, followed by a sixth line containing a name to search for. Display the position of that name in the list, counting from 1 (so the first name is position 1). If the name isn't in the list, display `Not found` instead.

For example, if the list is ada, alan, grace, lin, sam and the search name is grace, print 3 (grace is the third name).
hints: Python's list positions (indexes) count from 0, but this task wants positions counting from 1 — that's index + 1.
names = [], for i in range(5): names.append(input()), target = input(), if target in names: print(names.index(target) + 1), else: print("Not found")

tasks.title: Count above average
tasks.brief:
Six whole numbers are entered, one per line. Display how many of them are strictly greater than the mean (average) of all six.

For example, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 has a mean of 3.5 — three of the numbers (4, 5, 6) are greater than that, so print 3.
hints: Work out the mean of the whole list first — you need it before you can compare anything to it. Then loop through the list a second time to count.
numbers = [], for i in range(6): numbers.append(int(input())), mean = sum(numbers) / 6, count = 0, for n in numbers: if n > mean: count = count + 1

tasks.title: Second highest
tasks.brief:
Read five distinct whole numbers, one per line, into a list. Print the second highest value in the list — not the highest, the next one down.

For example, 3, 9, 1, 7, 5 has 9 as the highest and 7 as the second highest, so print 7.
hints: sorted(numbers, reverse=True) arranges a copy of the list from highest to lowest. The second highest is then sitting at index 1 (the highest is at index 0).
numbers = [], for i in range(5): numbers.append(int(input())), ordered = sorted(numbers, reverse=True), print(ordered[1])

tasks.title: Sorted scoreboard
tasks.brief: A games console stores the last five scores achieved by a player, entered one per line. Display the scores in order from highest to lowest, one per line. Then display a final line showing the average score, rounded to 1 decimal place.
hints: sorted(scores, reverse=True) sorts a list from highest to lowest in one step.
Average is the total of the list divided by how many items are in it — sum(scores) / len(scores)

tasks.title: Stock check
tasks.brief:
A shop stores the quantity in stock of six products, entered one per line as whole numbers. Any product with fewer than 5 items in stock needs reordering.

List the position (counting from 1) of each product that needs reordering, one per line. Then display the total number needing reorder, in the format `<count> to reorder`.

For example, if products 2 and 4 need reordering, print their positions (2, then 4), then print `2 to reorder`.
hints: Loop by index (using range(len(stock))) rather than by item, so you have the position available to print.
Count the matches in the same loop that checks and prints each low-stock position

tasks.title: Seating grid
tasks.brief:
A small cinema has 3 rows of 4 seats, stored as a 2D list. Read 12 values, one per line, reading across row 1 first, then row 2, then row 3. Each value is `X` for a taken seat or `-` for a free one.

Display the number of free seats in each row, one row per line, in the format `Row <n>: <count> free`.

For example, if row 1 has two free seats, print `Row 1: 2 free`.
hints: Build the 2D list with a loop inside a loop: an outer loop for each of the 3 rows, an inner loop reading 4 seats into that row.
For each row, count how many entries equal "-"

tasks.title: Sports day results
tasks.brief:
A school records the times of eight runners in a race. Each time is entered on its own line, as a whole number of seconds.

Produce a results summary of exactly three lines, in the format:

```
Winner time: 42
Slowest time: 61
Under 50: 3
```

`Under 50` is the number of runners whose time was less than 50 seconds.
hints: Read all eight times into a list first, before working out any of the three results.
min() and max() give the winner and slowest times directly; a counting loop gives the Under 50 figure

tasks.title: Club membership search
tasks.brief:
A club stores its members' names and ages in two separate lists that share the same positions — position 0 of each list refers to the same person.

Read 4 names, each followed on the next line by that member's age — the input alternates name, age, name, age, and so on.

After the data has been read, one more line is entered: a name to look up. Output either the age of that member, in the format `<name> is <age>`, or — if the name isn't in the list — the line `Not a member`.

The search is case sensitive ("Grace" and "grace" are different), and if a name appears twice, report the **first** match.

For example, searching for Grace after Grace was entered with age 24 prints `Grace is 24`.
hints: Append to two separate lists, names and ages, inside the same reading loop — one append to each list per pair of lines read.
Find the search name's index in the names list, then use that same index to look up the matching age

tasks.title: Tuck shop takings
tasks.brief:
A school tuck shop records how many items it sold of each of five products, along with the price of each product.

Read five lines, each containing the quantity sold. Then read five more lines, each containing the matching price, as a decimal.

Output two lines:
- the total takings for the day, rounded to 2 decimal places, in the format `Takings: <amount>`
- the position (counting from 1) of the product that earned the most, in the format `Best seller: <position>`

If two products earn exactly the same amount, report the earlier position.
hints: Read the quantities into one list and the prices into a second list — position 0 of each list refers to the same product.
Each product's takings is its quantity multiplied by its price; work these out into a third list, then use it to find both the total and the best seller

tasks.title: Class test averages
tasks.brief:
A teacher records the scores of 3 students, each of whom sat 3 tests — 9 values in total, read one per line, all of student 1's scores first, then all of student 2's, then all of student 3's.

For each student, print their average score rounded to 1 decimal place, in the format `Student <n>: <average>`. After all three, print which student had the highest average, in the format `Best: <n>`.

For example, if student 1 averages 60.0, student 2 averages 90.0, and student 3 averages 45.0, student 2 has the highest average.
hints: Build a 2D list: an outer loop for each of the 3 students, an inner loop reading that student's 3 scores into their own row.
Loop over the rows to print each average, keeping track of the highest average seen so far and which student it belongs to as you go
